title: Personal data; Finnish family background; journey to Washington
description: Claire Alexander fills out a personal data record with Sylvia Leaton, recording her birth in Butte, Montana in 1912, her maiden name Wayne, and her current address in Glenwood. Sylvia describes her Finnish father Charlie Wayne, who worked in Butte copper mines and died of miner's consumption, and her Swedish-Finnish grandparents who changed their name from Johnson. She recounts travelling to Washington by train at age five and the settlement of her mother's family in Hancock, Michigan.

title: Grandparents; mother's work; father's death
description: Sylvia gives details about her grandparents, including her grandmother who had 13 children and her grandfather who was a copper mine foreman in Michigan. Her mother worked as a department store clerk in Butte, where she met and married Charlie Wayne around 1910; after his death in 1922 from emphysema caused by mining, she worked as a housekeeper at Bridges Clinic in Tacoma and remarried.

title: Immediate family; Leighton ranch history
description: Sylvia names her sister Anita, half-brother Arnie Helene, husband William R. Leaton, and their three children Mary Anita, Claudia, and James Wayne. She recounts the Leighton family history: Bill's grandfather came from England, married a Michigan teacher, and homesteaded at Missouri Flats around 1905 after hearing about the Snowdon area; his wife wrote a poem describing their journey by boat to Lyle, the log cabin, and the loss of their cattle in a terrible storm the first winter.

title: Marriage and children
description: Sylvia was married to Bill in Poulsbo on June 26, 1941; their daughter Mary Anita was born June 29, 1942 in Hood River, Claudia on June 29, 1946 in Hood River, and son Jim on January 25, 1955 in The Dalles. Mary Anita is a housewife, Claudia works at Yakima Community College, and Jim runs a repair shop and partners with his father.

title: Education; teaching in Glenwood
description: Sylvia graduated from Lincoln High School in Tacoma in 1930 and the University of Puget Sound in 1935, working as a maid to pay tuition. She taught math and history at Vaughan for two years, then came to Glenwood in 1939 to teach home economics; she served as principal and teacher in a school with four teachers and 19 high school students, where students published a weekly paper, put on plays and carnivals, and played sports.

title: Community clubs; honors; National Science Foundation study
description: Sylvia describes belonging to Delta Kappa Gamma, Women's Club, Ladies Aid, Cowbells, and retired teachers groups, and helping raise money to remodel the church. She and Bill were named Cattlemen of the Year in 1966; she received National Science Foundation grants to study mathematics at the University of Vermont in 1966 and 1967.

title: Glenwood valley life; rural versus urban women
description: Sylvia finds Glenwood a wonderful place to raise children but misses city life, traffic, and rain, dislikes the snow and ice, and travels to White Salmon weekly to get out. She compares rural and urban women's lives, noting that rural women lack cultural access but that modern cars and roads make country living comparable to suburbs, and explains that ranchers are rich in assets but poor in cash.

title: Cooking for harvest crews; wartime rationing
description: Sylvia describes feeding 17 men for three days during oat combining and seven or eight men during haying, with help from Bill's aunt. During the war, sugar was rationed and she had to save sugar through the winter to bake four pies at noon and two cakes at supper for the harvest crews, with ranch families competing to set the best table.

title: Family life and childhood pastimes; Finnish community
description: Sylvia recalls mealtime conversations, card games, and extensive visiting among Finnish families where coffee and fresh baking were always served. Children played ball, hopscotch, and made mud cakes; Finnish dances lasted until daylight with lavish midnight buffets. She remembers being spanked in first grade and crying in Finnish, a language she can still understand but no longer speaks since her mother's death in 1961.

title: Teenage years; social life; attitudes toward sex and drugs
description: Sylvia describes making doll clothes at sixteen, then joining Glee Club, Girl Reserves, Girl Scouts, and sports in high school, where she had wanted to become a doctor until the Depression forced her to support herself through college. She recalls group parties without drinking, the presence of drug pushers outside schools, and her views that young people should be individuals and that sex should remain private and natural within marriage.

title: High school friends; household chores; gender roles
description: Sylvia's high school group included friends of German, English, and Irish backgrounds, mostly working class; her half-brother Arnie nearly married a judge's daughter until the girl's grandmother sent her to Europe. She describes her chores hanging clothes, washing windows, and carrying wood and coal, noting that her brother, born when she was in junior high, was spoiled by her mother and did no housework.

title: Courtship and marriage; meeting Bill; wedding; early economic struggles
description: Sylvia explains how she initially rejected marriage for teaching, then met Bill at a Glenwood dance after breaking off an earlier engagement. She describes their courtship, the impromptu wedding in Tacoma, and early marital conflicts over money and Bill's partnership with his uncle Frank.

title: Daily life without electricity; housing conditions; keeping warm
description: Sylvia describes their first home without electricity or running water, heating water on wood stoves, using kerosene lamps, and surviving a 45-below-zero winter with baby Mary Anita. She details the outhouse facilities and the Delco power plant that preceded rural electrification.

title: Social life and entertainment; community parties; cattle brands
description: The conversation turns to social activities including pinnacle parties, dances at various halls, and cattle association dinners where she learned to recognize her husband's brand. Sylvia contrasts the vibrant social life of the past with modern isolation.

title: Pregnancy and medical care; childbirth costs; spacing children
description: Sylvia discusses her prenatal care in Hood River, the doctors who delivered her three children, and how World War II affected their family planning. She reflects on having children in her thirties and forties.

title: Child rearing; discipline methods; raising children; babysitters
description: Sylvia explains her disciplinary philosophy of slapping hands rather than spanking, contrasting her methods with her sister's leniency and Mrs. Lofgren's permissiveness. She recounts her experience babysitting the Butler boy and later relying on babysitters while teaching.

title: Empty nest; aging; recreation and hobbies; current routines
description: Sylvia reflects on the trauma of children leaving home, the loneliness of aging, and her current lifestyle including extensive reading, crochet, dining out, and traveling with her sister.

title: Household work; washing diapers; working while mothering; teaching half days
description: Returning to the topic of child-rearing, Sylvia describes boiling diapers on wood stoves, washing clothes with ringer washers, and the grueling schedule of teaching while caring for infant Jim. She emphasizes her philosophy of never saying 'never' and trying new challenges.

title: Home utilities; indoor plumbing; heating and cooking; farm labor
description: Leaton explains that her home obtained electricity in 1941 and indoor plumbing in 1946, describing the use of outhouses and a wood box built into the kitchen wall. She details the transition from wood stoves to oil heaters and the division of labor involving wood cutting and animal care on the farm.

title: Cow camp life; mountain access; Depression impact; domestic service; views on wealth
description: She describes the traditional cow camp where a banker and judge perform their own chores, and notes that current mountain conditions require radio contact for access. Leaton reflects on how the Great Depression fostered her independence despite losing savings, recalls her domestic service for the Butler family in Tacoma, and shares a philosophy on wealth learned from Mrs. Pickham.

title: Mattson kidnapping; teaching retirement; scientific progress; youth suicide; alcohol and food
description: Leaton recounts the kidnapping and murder of the Mattson boy during the Depression, linking it to the dangers of wealth. She discusses missing her teaching career, organizing luncheons for retired teachers, and witnessing major scientific events including the moon landing and Mount St. Helens eruption. The section concludes with discussion of student Kenny Feller's suicide, community alcohol issues, and food.
